plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional surface plot enclosed in a thin rectangular wireframe box, with no axis labels, tick marks, or numerical scales shown. A broad flat blue sheet spans the box at mid-height, standing for the level far from the charges. On the right half of the sheet the surface rises into a steep, narrow peak whose flanks are banded in pink and violet and whose tip is cut off flat. On the left half the surface plunges into a matching funnel-shaped depression, shaded the same way and likewise truncated at its base. Dark contour lines run across the surface as closed loops encircling both the peak and the pit, crowding together where the surface steepens and spreading into wide rounded loops out on the flat sheet, with a faint straight line crossing the sheet between the two features. Rendering potential as height converts the sign and size of the potential into visible relief, so the hill and the trough can be read against each other directly. The plot builds intuition for the potential of two equal and opposite charges carried on conducting spheres of finite radius.

elements: thin rectangular wireframe box enclosing the plot volume, no axes, ticks, or labels
broad flat sheet at mid-height (V=0 reference level) spanning the box floor
3D potential surface: steep truncated peak (pink/violet) on the right half around the positive charge
matching truncated funnel-shaped depression on the left half around the negative charge
dark contour lines on the surface: closed loops crowding near peak and pit, spreading wide on the flat sheet
faint straight line across the sheet connecting the two charge sites (V=0 nodal line region)
small sphere markers indicating the two conducting charge positions (positive right, negative left)
flat 2D contour-map view (top-down) with the same closed loops, shown when contour view is active

interactions.label: Charge ratio q−/q+
interactions.teaches: Varying the relative source strengths changes the peak and well depths: equal and opposite charges give symmetric hill and trough, while a weaker negative charge gives a shallower trough, revealing how potential sign and magnitude follow the source charges

interactions.label: Charge separation d
interactions.teaches: Moving the charges apart or together shifts the hill, trough, and contour loops; close charges produce strong cancellation with a steep saddle between them, showing how superposed potentials shape the region between the spheres

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching between relief and top-down contour views shows the same information two ways: crowded contour loops correspond exactly to the steep flanks of the peak and pit, i.e. strong potential gradient (strong field)
Rotating the relief plot makes the height-as-potential encoding tangible — the hill and trough can be compared in depth from any angle

demo_steps.title: Equal and opposite charges
demo_steps.narration: With q−/q+ = −1 the peak and pit are mirror images, and the contour loops are symmetric about the center line. Height reads directly as potential.

demo_steps.title: Unbalanced charges
demo_steps.narration: Reduce the negative charge magnitude toward zero: the trough shallows and its loops spread out while the positive peak stays tall — potential magnitude tracks source strength.

demo_steps.title: Bring the charges together
demo_steps.narration: Decrease separation: hill and trough approach, loops crowd in the gap, and far away the surface flattens — the dipole potential falls off faster than a single charge's.

demo_steps.title: Contour view
demo_steps.narration: Flatten to the top-down contour map: the same loops, crowded near each charge and sparse far away — dense contours mean steep potential and strong electric field.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Potential of two charges: V(x,y) = k*q+ / max(r+, rMin) + k*q− / max(r−, rMin), with q+ = +1 fixed and q− set by the charge-ratio slider (−1 to 0). Charges sit on the x-axis at (±d/2, 0), d from separation slider (default d=3, so at x=±1.5). rMin ≈ 0.35 truncates the singularities, producing the flat-topped peak and flat-bottomed pit (representing finite conducting spheres). Domain: x ∈ [−3.5, 3.5], y ∈ [−2.6, 2.6] world units, sampled on a ~90×70 grid. Height scale: map V=±1 to ±0.9 world units; the mid-plane z=0 sheet is implicit in the surface's flat region. Wireframe box: ~7.4 × 5.6 footprint, 2.6 tall, drawn as thin grey edges around the surface. Positive charge site at RIGHT (+x), negative at LEFT, matching the source image. Colors: base sheet light blue #7fb2e5; peak bands pink #e8a0c0 to violet #9b6bb8; pit uses the same pink/violet shading on its inner flanks; contour lines dark navy #1a2a4a; charge markers small red (+) and dark blue (−) spheres ~0.12 radius at the truncation centers.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the surface as a ParametricGeometry/BufferGeometry recomputed on any slider change; vertex-color by height (blue at 0 → pink/violet at extremes, same palette above and below as in the source). Contours: draw ~14 level curves (marching-squares on the potential grid or THREE.Line loops at fixed V levels) as dark lines slightly above the surface. Contour Map toggle: animate camera to top-down (elevation 90) and flatten/swap the surface for a flat colored plane with the same contour lines; keep both representations precomputed and toggle visibility. Orbit disabled while in Contour Map (or limited to pan/zoom) to preserve the flat-map reading.

authoredContext:
To improve your intuition, we show a three-dimensional variant of the potential in a system with two opposing charges. The figure displays a three-dimensional map of electric potential, where lines on the map are for equipotential surfaces. The hill is at the positive charge, and the trough is at the negative charge. The potential is zero far away from the charges. Note that the cut off at a particular potential implies that the charges are on conducting spheres with a finite radius.

Electric potential map of two opposite charges of equal magnitude on conducting spheres. The potential is negative near the negative charge and positive near the positive charge.

The illustration shows electric potential map and equipotential lines two charges – one positive and one negative.

A two-dimensional map of the cross-sectional plane that contains both charges is shown in the figure. The line that is equidistant from the two opposite charges corresponds to zero potential, since at the points on the line, the positive potential from the positive charge cancels the negative potential from the negative charge. Equipotential lines in the cross-sectional plane are closed loops, which are not necessarily circles, since at each point, the net potential is the sum of the potentials from each charge.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Potential of two charges: V(x,y) = k*q+ / max(r+, rMin) + k*q− / max(r−, rMin), with q+ = +1 fixed and q− set by the charge-ratio slider (−1 to 0). Charges sit on the x-axis at (±d/2, 0), d from separation slider (default d=3, so at x=±1.5). rMin ≈ 0.35 truncates the singularities, producing the flat-topped peak and flat-bottomed pit (representing finite conducting spheres). Domain: x ∈ [−3.5, 3.5], y ∈ [−2.6, 2.6] world units, sampled on a ~90×70 grid. Height scale: map V=±1 to ±0.9 world units; the mid-plane z=0 sheet is implicit in the surface's flat region. Wireframe box: ~7.4 × 5.6 footprint, 2.6 tall, drawn as thin grey edges around the surface. Positive charge site at RIGHT (+x), negative at LEFT, matching the source image. Colors: base sheet light blue #7fb2e5; peak bands pink #e8a0c0 to violet #9b6bb8; pit uses the same pink/violet shading on its inner flanks; contour lines dark navy #1a2a4a; charge markers small red (+) and dark blue (−) spheres ~0.12 radius at the truncation centers.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the surface as a ParametricGeometry/BufferGeometry recomputed on any slider change; vertex-color by height (blue at 0 → pink/violet at extremes, same palette above and below as in the source). Contours: draw ~14 level curves (marching-squares on the potential grid or THREE.Line loops at fixed V levels) as dark lines slightly above the surface. Contour Map toggle: animate camera to top-down (elevation 90) and flatten/swap the surface for a flat colored plane with the same contour lines; keep both representations precomputed and toggle visibility. Orbit disabled while in Contour Map (or limited to pan/zoom) to preserve the flat-map reading.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a single three-dimensional surface plot enclosed in a thin rectangular wireframe box, with no axis labels, tick marks, or numerical scales shown. A broad flat blue sheet spans the box at mid-height, standing for the level far from the charges. On the right half of the sheet the surface rises into a steep, narrow peak whose flanks are banded in pink and violet and whose tip is cut off flat. On the left half the surface plunges into a matching funnel-shaped depression, shaded the same way and likewise truncated at its base. Dark contour lines run across the surface as closed loops encircling both the peak and the pit, crowding together where the surface steepens and spreading into wide rounded loops out on the flat sheet, with a faint straight line crossing the sheet between the two features. Rendering potential as height converts the sign and size of the potential into visible relief, so the hill and the trough can be read against each other directly. The plot builds intuition for the potential of two equal and opposite charges carried on conducting spheres of finite radius.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for charge balance: vary the positive and negative source strengths and the surface peak/well heights update, showing electric potential sign and relative magnitude.
- Toggle between surface and contour views: the learner switches representations, the raised/lowered surface flattens into contour loops with the same crowded spacing near charges, showing that steep height changes correspond to strong potential gradients.
- Slider for charge separation: the learner moves the equal and opposite charges apart or together, the hill, trough, and contour loops shift accordingly, clarifying how superposed potentials shape the region between conducting spheres.
